Empire is definitely one of my favourite titles in the Total War series but for a lot of TW gamers I talk to they don't often understand why. Empire ranks fairly low in terms of reception alongside other contemporary titles despite being the only TW game set in the Georgian era. I'm going to avoid doing a huge broad review of the game, and instead focus on two points I'd like to raise for the new player:

1) The battle engine

This gets a lot of hate right off the bat. Essentially, before Empire if you charged two units of infantry together in any preceding game they would smush into a realistic mass and start going to town on one another. If four of your guys surrounded one of the enemy, they would all attack together and punch his lights out. Since the Warscape engine was introduced with Empire, the combat is reduced to kill moves only. This means that only one soldier can kill any one other soldier at any one time, and it is based on pre-scripted and often quite lengthy kill moves. Combine this with a very badly-designed unit collision system? If you look at a melee battle, it's like watching Cheerios with ADHD fight for control of the milk.

Empire does reduce this impact somewhat. With the basis being on firelock warfare above everything else, the vast majority of your battles on this game are going to be conducted at range with the major exception of cavalry charges. The engine is nowhere near as prominent in this scenario, and I actually think the musket volleys look great when they pick out six or seven blokes from across the enemy's front line. I cannot excuse the melee though, it just looks awful.

2) Campaign Diplomacy

The campaign itself was a lot of fun for me. I found the politics system a little dry and underused, but aside from the occasional spot of lag the campaign map was by and large really enjoyable. I have played a Swedish and Prussian game recently and really enjoyed both aside from one thing: the diplomacy.

The diplomacy makes no sense. The AI factions ask for backwater regions all the time, they refuse alliances and trade agreements for no good reason, the factors influencing international reputation are incredibly difficult to manipulate and almost impossible to move back to positive/negative after they have gone too far in either direction and above all it just lacks any kind of logic and breaks the immersion. 



There are tons more pros and cons to the game, but I felt I'd keep my review nice and concise and focus on the two biggest deal breakers for me. Even with those in full effect, I still love this game and have great fun both on single and multiplayer. I'd recommend it for sure!

So, you want to conquer the world? Here's the major nations you're up against:

Great Britain: hide your port cities, because these guys want them

Ottoman Empire: thinks that spamming artillery is a great strategy 
Austria: thinks that spamming light infantry is a great strategy 
Poland: has a boring roster with no gimmicks, so naturally, it will become the dominant power in Eastern/Central Europe 
Russia: is Poland's attack dog 
Spain: takes anyone owning anything in America as a personal insult
Sweden: starts with no allies and will die with no allies
USA: you'll completely forget these guys exist until the late game, when Maryland rebels against Great Britain, and promptly dies soon after
Mughal Empire: who?
United Provinces (Dutch): either dies within the first 30 turns, or somehow takes over Western Europe
Maratha Confederacy: the true final boss of Empire Total War
 
EDIT: Alright, folks, don't forget the little guys you'll be up against too: The Minor Nations

Barbary States: these guys will be the 2nd most annoying faction for you to deal with, until they get colonized by Sweden of all things
Bavaria: Austria's hype man 
Cherokee Nations: sandwiched between Spain and Great Britain and dies as fast as you'd think 
Courland: Poland's protectorate which is really just a doormat for Sweden 
Crimean Khanate: Don't you mean, Russia? 
Georgia and Dagestan: two minor nations with the greatest of bromances in this game, built on a mutual hatred of Russia 
Denmark: will lose their homeland to Sweden before retreating to Iceland where they will hide for the rest of the game 
Genoa: Spain's #1 lackey 
Hannover: Literally the only minor nation that usually allies with Prussia, naturally they don't last long 
Huron Confederacy: a Native American faction whose best defense is being so obscure everyone forgets about them 
Inuit Nations: refer to above description 
Iroquois Confederacy: sandwiched between Great Britain and France; the question is, will they outlast the Cherokee? 
Italian States: is basically just Rome and is a nostalgia target for all Rome: Total War players 
Knights of St. John: Despite being a single island right in the middle of the mosh pit that is the Mediterranean Sea, this faction will survive until the end of the game
Louisiana, New Spain, and 13 Colonies: literally exist just to assimilate into their respective overlords within the first few turns
Morocco: a great minor nation with an awesome starting province, it just has the terrible disadvantage of being neighbors with Spain 
Mysore: that kid in the group project that does absolutely nothing but still gets a good grade, in this case, thanks to the Maratha Confederacy 
Persia: Place your bets, will they die to the Ottomans or the Maratha Confederacy?

Two major bugs that I have run into that seriously hamper the game to this day:
1) If you defeat Great Britain in Europe, the USA can spawn from its colonies as an independent nation. I have run into issues where after several endturns later on the United States' turn the game will crash with no real way of circumventing it, effectively bricking your entire campaign.
2) Offensive fort siege battles can get unplayably sluggish and this is my observation as to why: After making a breach in a fortress siege battle the defending AI will rapidly give its units the same orders and will not stop. Performance decreases as this process goes on so it becomes a race against the game's dwindling frames-per-second to take the fort before the game becomes an unplayable slideshow.
Normally I would be an advocate for Empire because of the novelty of its campaign map stretching across much of the world, but the developer's recent interest in marketing and promoting Empire without taking the time to fix the game-breaking issues that cripple it to this day compels me to let people know about the serious technical issues that plague this game.

I’m a fan of [i]Rome[/i] and the [i]Medieval[/i] entries in this series, and I approached this installment with the same enthusiasm—back on an old computer and before the Steam days (that’s why I don’t have hundreds of hours logged in this game—unfortunately).

This game has the power to draw you in for dozens upon dozens of sessions. The naval battles are outstanding, and it captures the spirit of the era beautifully. In essence, [i]Creative Assembly[/i] took the best from their previous games, polished the graphics, and staged a massive conflict across Europe and its colonies. The game is tougher, with more emphasis on economy and diplomacy. The tech tree takes some getting used to—it initially struck me as a “throwback innovation,” but it's a deep system worth mastering.

The level of detail and craftsmanship in the units is superb, and the threat of revolutions adds an exciting layer. There’s a unique thrill in reaching the Ural Mountains and subduing every nation along the way.

This is the game where management became as captivating as building up an army and waging wars. It's a fantastic installment, but you’ll need to set aside time during a vacation or a break to truly enjoy it.

This is widely criticized as one of the buggiest titles in the series and often called one of the worst overall. I wholeheartedly disagree with the latter.

While this title is certainly buggy at times, it performs very well and provides some of the most entertaining total war battles to date. The naval battles are second only to Napoleon (and to be honest I didn't really put much time into Napoleon so I really should not count that title). The land battles are capable of being incredibly large and exceptionally exciting. The AI isn't the best in the series but I find it good enough to provide a challenge.

Overall, the game looks and sounds great. The game may crash on rare occasions as many games will eventually do but this one has a greater tendency to run for hours without trouble on all of the systems I have ever played it on. The game's DLC isn't all that great but what really matters is the base campaign which is awesome fun.

Compared to other games in the series, this one has the largest playable campaign map with regions stretching as far west as the American mid-west and as far east as India. The naval battles are so good you will actually WANT to play them...most of the time...they will admittedly get a big tedious later on when you have 20 or more ships under your command.

Overall I feel this game is largely over-criticized because it was the first in the series built on the newer game engine which frustrated a lot of the old school fans. While I still prefer Medieval 2 to this title, I still enjoy this title today and can't wait for an Empire 2.

EDIT: I would like to add that just when I thought I had grown out of this game, I discovered an overhaul called Durango mod. It is a sort of "Empire Vanilla+" which overhauls the game without adding too much unnecessary complexity. The game is now better than ever and is essentially the way it was meant to be. It feels significantly less buggy and is so much more fun to play. You can't download the mod from any mod site though, so you'll need to contact the mod creator directly and get a direct link for it.

While I love it, it must be said. This game is absolute trash. It's an unfinished beta of a game that wanted to be too much, in a time when development was harsh and unforgiving, under the direction of a new publisher that most likely moved all of the staff from Australia to Britain, cancelling a great deal of what was being prepared in the meantime, reorganizing personnel hastly and \ or with terrible timing and awful decision making.
While at its core Creative Assembly was still MTW2's old crew, many - including the battle mechanics programmer - went away mid development. This disorganization coupled with absurdly placed goals and SEGA's demands, created the perfect storm. Empire Total War is the result of a small studio being acquired by a greater entity and put on a forced march towards glory; they needed to literally touch the Sun, and just like Icarus, they failed and landed on their head back to Earth.

Up until mid 2011 - release was March 2009 - the game was borderline unplayable. For well over 2 years musketeers wheeling into the foreground with no AI, terrible campaign crashes, endless loading times, and a plethora of bugs and glitches made the experience awful. But the scope and the novelty of such an endeavour still attracted masses of casuals and the most hardcore groups of exploiters went on to form elite squads of competitive ETW gamers. I was in one too at the time, an international competitive group with a strong German presence. For almost 3 years we got together every week to ruin everyone's fun because winning in this game was - and still is - totally based on exploits. Units have godawful balancing, the speed and impact of all cavalry is all over the place; you can place 2 rows of light cavalrymen behind your infantry and have 3 volleys of instant fire that WILL destroy any unit present beside Guards. If you were a newbie, or even an intermediate player, you'd be completely screwed in a competitive setting, and even at a casual level, the amount of exploits was so atrocious you'd be a winner even in a 2 v 1 secnario just because you'd be making  a 10 Guards 10 Artillery army and flood people with mortar fire. Ragequitting was the norm for everyone. Netcode has always been awful to the core. The few people that still play it in MP know every nook and cranny and can destroy anybody with a thought because all of these incredibly frustrating balancing choices are still there.

The SP side isnt any better tho. AI is an absolute mess of convoluted nonsense. Coding and optimization of the campaign map and battle maps is so bad that it hurts even modern PCs. 
MP campaign was in development and testing phase but again, since this mess of a game came out rushing in through the door with at least 1 year of development left in the dumpster, the few lucky ones able to actually play any game got crashes upon crashes and loading a saved game even with perfect syncing would result in freezes as soon as you'd press the end turn button.
There is STILL an unavoidable, random crash in the Ottoman's turn after 11 years. Never patched, never fixed. The last patch they applied in 2011, while stabilizing the game a bit, completely destroyed the first person camera's coding. You cannot view the bullet trajectory anymore, not from muskets nor from cannons. The game just freezes mid-air.
Switzerland was planned and half finished in the code, but you cant enable it back. Pieces of development tools never given to the public were also half finished and thrown in the dumpster, waiting to be released only in late 2012 for Shogun 2.

I spent an ungodly amount of hours playing this game. I enjoyed it, but I wouldnt recommend it to anyone. It was amazing the first time I put my eyes on it back in 2009, and the few years I went nuts with all the exploits and a crew of dedicated companions to fight with. But now.... no, absolutely not. This game has been abandoned and left in a sorry state for a decade, the only thing keeping it somewhat alive are mods, and even those cant pull its butt up from the ground. There's no sendoff, no fanfare, and there never will be. The creators didnt love their baby enough, and put their necks on a yoke in servitude of SEGA's ambitions. There is no pity, nor remorse in here. Naiveté got their hands in the dirt. Few years later, with Rome 2, they'd prove themselves to be in the same situation. But that is a story for another time.

Empire sits at the crossroads of the series where player autonomy began to be taken away, while at the same time CA made great additions to the formula in an ambitious and exciting setting.

Pros:
- The gunpowder line warfare works really well with a Total War (TW) game & allows for a very rewarding sense of racing for knowledge in the enlightenment to gain an economic or military edge over your enemies
- You can play across the world with robust trading systems and incentives to play the great naval battles
- Unlike most other TW games, the map comes alive through new towns emerging allowing you to build an empire from the ground up in a manner you like. There could be more variety with the building choices here though.
- Being able to build and upgrade roads weirdly enough, then see them on the campaign map as they boost population numbers and trade. There is a real feeling of building your empire from the ground up
- You can build forts anywhere on the map instead of the unfortunate new "pre assigned spot" system used by CA
- Total army movement freedom where each unit can be stationed to guard a specific choke point or travel between armies. This is a very old and fixable ai problem please bring this back with new releases CA!

Cons:
- Player choice was reduced in the types of buildings you can put in each region. The original Rome TW was iconic partly because you could conquer any part of the map you liked and build it into a commercial or military capital of your empire in the long term & you then got to see each new building by entering an immersive view mode
- Playing as Russia is actually extremely rewarding and fun with the region growth mechanics and their hybrid roster
- The combat can feel clunky and outdated especially in melee or siege engagements 

I still enjoy coming back to this game more than playing some of the newest historical releases because of the region growth and army management game design choices. I also find in the era before automatic unit replenishment, it incentivizes you to find the best tactics possible to avoid paying unit replenishment costs. Overall, although Empire is less polished than other TW titles, it is still worth playing. This game really goes to show how well an Empire 2 would do with a modern engine that handles moving from gunpowder to melee more gracefully while still keeping the player freedom that their old core fanbase so dearly miss.
